notes:
Task and constraints: Count triples of indices whose positive side lengths can form a triangle.
Idea: Sort the side lengths, then for each largest side use two pointers to count pairs whose sum exceeds it.
Technique and why it applies: If nums[left]+nums[right] exceeds nums[i], every index between left and right-1 also forms a valid pair with right, so right-left triples are added at once. Otherwise left advances to increase the sum.
Invariant: For each fixed largest side nums[i], left and right delimit pairs not yet counted or rejected by the triangle inequality.
Edge cases: Zero sides are naturally excluded by the strict inequality. Sorting mutates nums, and duplicate values at different indices count as distinct triples.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), and the two-pointer scan for each i is O(n), giving O(n²) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond sorting.

Task and constraints: Schedule tasks with a cooldown of n intervals between identical task types and minimize total intervals.
Idea: Use a max-heap of remaining task frequencies and a queue holding tasks that are cooling down until their release time.
Technique and why it applies: Each time unit executes the most frequent available task, decrements its count, and queues any remaining copies with release time timer+n. A task re-enters the heap when its cooldown expires.
Invariant: max_heap contains available task counts; queue stores remaining counts and their earliest next execution time.
Edge cases: If no task is available while the queue is nonempty, the timer still advances, accounting for idle intervals. The snippet uses deque, defaultdict, and heappush/heappop without importing them, so those names must be provided externally.
Complexity: For T tasks and A distinct types, heap and queue operations take O(T log A) time and O(A) space, aside from idle time steps represented by timer increments.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum product obtainable from any three numbers in nums.
Idea: Sort descending and compare the product of the three largest values with the product of the two smallest and the largest.
Technique and why it applies: The optimum either uses the three largest values or combines two large-magnitude negatives, whose positive product can exceed the product of the top three. The larger of these two candidates is returned.
Invariant: After sorting, nums[0:3] are the three largest values and nums[-2:] are the two smallest values.
Edge cases: Negative values and zeros are handled by the two candidate products. The problem guarantees at least three elements.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n) time and mutates nums in place; the calculation uses O(1) additional space. The comments' O(1) space label ignores any implementation-dependent sorting workspace.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum product of any three elements in the array.
Idea: Track the two smallest values and three largest values in a single pass, then compare the two possible maximum products.
Technique and why it applies: A maximum product can come from three large positives or from the largest value multiplied by two large-magnitude negatives. The maintained extrema cover both cases without sorting.
Invariant: min1/min2 are the two smallest values seen, and max1/max2/max3 are the three largest values seen.
Edge cases: The array has at least three elements. The <= and >= comparisons correctly preserve repeated equal extrema.
Complexity: Each element updates a fixed number of scalar values, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of length n with exactly k inverse pairs, modulo 1,000,000,007.
Idea: Use a one-dimensional DP and a sliding prefix sum to compute each new permutation length's inverse-pair counts.
Technique and why it applies: Inserting the next largest value can add between zero and i inverse pairs. The running sum adds the previous DP values in that window and subtracts the value that falls outside it.
Invariant: dp[j] is the number of permutations of the current size with exactly j inverse pairs, modulo the constant.
Edge cases: k=0 yields one increasing permutation. The loop's range(n) processes each added value once; the tab/space mixture in a comment may be a formatting issue but is not part of the algorithm.
Complexity: The DP processes n rows of k+1 states, giving O(nk) time and O(k) space.

Task and constraints: Count arrays that are permutations of 1..n with exactly k inverse pairs, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Update a DP array using the prefix-sum recurrence for inserting each new largest value.
Technique and why it applies: new_dp[j] starts with dp[j], adds the previous new_dp[j-1] prefix contribution, and subtracts dp[j-(i+1)] when that value leaves the allowed insertion window.
Invariant: dp[j] counts permutations of the previous size with j inverse pairs; new_dp[j] counts them after adding the next value.
Edge cases: k=0 remains one, corresponding to the sorted permutation. The imported reduce function is unused.
Complexity: Each of n iterations updates k+1 entries, so time is O(nk) and space is O(k).

Task and constraints: Return the number of permutations with exactly k inverse pairs for size n, modulo 1,000,000,007.
Idea: Use a rolling prefix sum over the previous DP row to generate the next row.
Technique and why it applies: curr accumulates counts dp[j] and removes dp[j-(i+1)] once the insertion-window width is exceeded. Each state therefore sums exactly the prior counts that can lead to j inverse pairs after inserting the next largest element.
Invariant: curr equals the sliding window sum for the current j, and new_dp[j] stores that value modulo MOD.
Edge cases: The initial row has one way to form zero inverse pairs and none for positive counts. The reduce import is unused.
Complexity: Each DP row is computed in O(k) time, for O(nk) total time and O(k) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: The stated task counts permutations with exactly k inverse pairs, but this variant explicitly constructs candidate permutations.
Idea: Maintain lists of permutations grouped by inverse-pair count, inserting a new value into prior candidates at positions derived from the current loop variables.
Technique and why it applies: The nested comprehensions generate candidate lists for each DP bucket, then an assertion checks the inverse-pair count of candidates in the final bucket before returning its size modulo MOD.
Invariant: dp[j] is intended to contain candidate permutations with j inverse pairs after each value is introduced.
Edge cases: This construction is highly nonstandard and the assertion compares each generated permutation's count against len(dp)-1, the target k. It may be prohibitively expensive and should not be treated as a conventional verified DP.
Complexity: The number of explicitly stored permutations can grow combinatorially, so time and space can be exponential or factorial in n rather than O(nk).

Task and constraints: Count permutations with a specified number of inverse pairs, using an explicit permutation-construction approach.
Idea: Keep candidate permutations grouped by inverse-pair count and insert each new integer into each earlier candidate at positions intended to create a target count.
Technique and why it applies: The nested list comprehensions produce variants of each candidate list for each target bucket. The assertion then checks whether each generated permutation has the requested inverse-pair count.
Invariant: dp[j] is intended to hold all candidate permutations with j inverse pairs for the values processed so far.
Edge cases: Explicitly enumerating permutations can explode in size. The assertion and insertion-index expression are unusual and may not correctly establish the DP invariant; this is an exploratory implementation, not an efficient standard recurrence.
Complexity: Candidate counts can be factorial in n, so both time and space can grow combinatorially and are much larger than O(nk).

Task and constraints: Count permutations of 1..n with exactly k inverse pairs modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Apply the insertion recurrence with a list comprehension and reduce over the possible numbers of new inverse pairs.
Technique and why it applies: For each new size and target j, the code sums prior dp[j-k] values for k in the allowed range, counting every possible insertion position for the new largest value.
Invariant: dp[j] holds the number of permutations of the current size with j inverse pairs after each outer iteration.
Edge cases: The dp array is limited to k+1 entries, so only requested counts through k are retained. The imported reduce is used for every state calculation.
Complexity: Each of n rows computes k+1 states, and each state may sum O(n) prior states, giving O(n²k) time in the worst case and O(k) space; this explains the TLE tag.

Task and constraints: Return the count of permutations with exactly k inverse pairs.
Idea: Use a sliding-window DP, allowing the array to grow only to the maximum inverse-pair count possible for the current permutation size.
Technique and why it applies: Each new largest element can create at most i new inverse pairs, so the next row has at most the previous length plus i entries. The recurrence adds the previous prefix count and subtracts the value leaving the window.
Invariant: dp[j] counts permutations of the current size with j inverse pairs, and entries beyond the current maximum are not stored.
Edge cases: If k is larger than the final DP array length, the method returns zero. k=0 remains one for every positive n.
Complexity: The total number of updated states is O(min(k,n²)·n) as a coarse bound, with O(k) maximum DP storage. More tightly, each of n rows processes at most min(k+1, i(i+1)/2+1) states.

Task and constraints: Schedule the maximum number of courses, each with a duration and deadline, starting at time zero and taking courses sequentially.
Idea: Sort courses by deadline, add each duration to a max-heap, and remove the longest selected course whenever the accumulated time exceeds the current deadline.
Technique and why it applies: Considering courses in deadline order preserves feasibility for earlier deadlines. If the schedule is too long, dropping the longest duration frees the most time while retaining the maximum possible number of courses.
Invariant: now is the total duration of selected courses, and max_heap stores their durations as negative values.
Edge cases: Courses are sorted in place. The heap can contain zero courses if no feasible course remains; the result is the number of retained courses.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), and each course causes at most one heap insertion and one removal, so time is O(n log n) and space O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the smallest inclusive range containing at least one value from each of k sorted lists.
Idea: Maintain the current smallest value from each list in a min-heap and track the largest value among the selected elements.
Technique and why it applies: The heap minimum is the current range's left endpoint and right is the largest current endpoint. Popping the minimum and advancing within its list is the only way to potentially shrink the left boundary; if that list ends, no further complete range can be formed.
Invariant: The heap contains one current element from every list, and [heap_min,right] covers all those values.
Edge cases: The method assumes every list is nonempty because it reads row[0]. It updates the answer only for a strictly smaller width, preserving the first range among equal-width candidates.
Complexity: Each list element is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(N log k) time and O(k) heap space for N total elements.

Task and constraints: Determine whether nonnegative integer c can be expressed as a²+b² for integers a and b.
Idea: Try every a whose square does not exceed c and test whether the square root of c-a² is an integer.
Technique and why it applies: For each candidate a, a valid b must satisfy b²=c-a². math.sqrt computes the candidate root, and is_integer checks whether it is whole.
Invariant: Every a from zero through floor(sqrt(c)) is examined, so a successful return identifies a valid sum of two squares.
Edge cases: c=0 returns True because a=0 and b=0 succeed. Floating-point square roots can theoretically be affected by precision for large integers, though common constraints are small enough for this approach.
Complexity: There are O(sqrt(c)) candidates, each using constant-time arithmetic under fixed-width assumptions, so time is O(sqrt(c)) and space O(1).

Task and constraints: Check whether c is the sum of two integer squares.
Idea: Enumerate a from zero to floor(sqrt(c)), compute the integer square root of the remainder, and test the exact sum.
Technique and why it applies: If c-a² is a perfect square, then its integer square root b satisfies a²+b²=c. The explicit equality avoids accepting a non-square remainder.
Invariant: Each iteration checks one candidate a, and no smaller a has produced a valid pair if the loop continues.
Edge cases: c=0 returns True at a=0. c is nonnegative under the problem constraints, so sqrt(c) is defined.
Complexity: The loop has O(sqrt(c)) iterations and constant auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the exclusive execution time of each function from nested start/end logs.
Idea: Use a stack of active function IDs and start timestamps, assigning elapsed time to the current top when calls begin or end.
Technique and why it applies: A start event charges the parent for time since its last start point and pushes the child. An end event charges the child inclusively through its end timestamp, then advances the parent's start marker to timestamp+1.
Invariant: The stack's top is the currently executing function, and its stored timestamp is the first unit of time not yet charged to that function.
Edge cases: End timestamps are inclusive, so the code adds one. Logs are assumed properly nested and chronologically ordered.
Complexity: Each log causes constant work and each function call is pushed and popped once, giving O(L) time and O(D) stack space for L logs and maximum depth D.

Task and constraints: Return each function's exclusive runtime from a chronological log of nested calls.
Idea: Track the active function stack and the previous timestamp not yet accounted for.
Technique and why it applies: On start, the active parent receives the interval from prev up to but excluding the new start time. On end, the top function receives the inclusive interval through the end timestamp, and prev advances one unit beyond it.
Invariant: prev is the first timestamp not yet charged to the active stack, and stk records the nesting order of function IDs.
Edge cases: End logs add one to include the ending time unit. The input is assumed valid, with each end matching the most recent start.
Complexity: One pass over L logs gives O(L) time and O(D) auxiliary stack space.

Task and constraints: Minimize the cost of buying exactly the requested quantities using individual prices and special bundle offers.
Idea: Recursively try each offer that does not exceed current needs and is cheaper than buying its items separately, memoizing by the remaining-needs tuple.
Technique and why it applies: The baseline is buying all remaining items individually. Each valid offer reduces needs and adds its price to the recursive optimum; the minimum of these options is stored.
Invariant: memo[needs] is intended to hold the minimum cost to satisfy that remaining quantity vector.
Edge cases: The default memo={} is shared across separate calls to this nested function, and the key omits price and special; calling the method on different inputs can therefore reuse stale results incorrectly. The problem's offers are assumed to have nonnegative quantities.
Complexity: With memoization, the number of states is bounded by the product of (needs[i]+1), and each state tests all offers. Space is proportional to the number of cached states, excluding recursive frames.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum cost to fulfill needs using single-item prices and any number of special offers.
Idea: Recursively decide how many times to use each special offer, then price remaining items individually after all offers are considered.
Technique and why it applies: At each offer index, the code first explores skipping that offer. It then subtracts the offer quantities and, if needs remain nonnegative, recurses at the same index to allow reusing that offer; needs are restored afterward.
Invariant: Each recursive state returns the minimum cost using offers from index i onward for the current needs vector.
Edge cases: The code assumes every offer consumes at least one item; an all-zero offer could recurse without reducing needs. It mutates needs temporarily but restores each coordinate before returning.
Complexity: The search may explore many combinations of offer counts, exponential in the number of feasible combinations. Recursion depth is bounded by total offer uses plus the number of offer types; auxiliary space follows that depth.

Task and constraints: Count decodings of a string containing digits and '*' wildcards, where each letter maps to 1 through 26, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Use dynamic programming with counts for single-character and two-character interpretations, including wildcard multiplicities.
Technique and why it applies: cMap records how many letters each one- or two-character pattern can represent. For each position, dp combines decodings ending with one character and those ending with a valid pair.
Invariant: dp[i] stores the number of decodings for the prefix ending at position i-1, with the final slot used as the empty-prefix base.
Edge cases: A leading zero returns zero immediately. The check that returns zero whenever a DP value is zero is unsafe after modulo reduction: a valid count can be congruent to zero modulo MOD while later two-character contributions make the final answer nonzero.
Complexity: The map is constant-sized and each character is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(n) DP space.
